book.title: Some People Need Killing: A Memoir of Murder in My Country

evidence: trade publisher signal: Random House / Penguin Random House

argument.statement: An elected president’s “war on drugs” created a reign of terror in which some lives were treated as worth less than others, enabling widespread killings by police and vigilantes.

book.rationale: The book is a journalistic account focused on the political violence and state-sanctioned killings under Duterte's regime in the Philippines, making Journalism & Reportage the primary subject, while also addressing significant themes in Politics & Government and True Crime & Justice.
book.summary: TIME’S #1 NONFICTION BOOK OF THE YEAR • A NEW YORK TIMES BOOK REVIEW TOP 10 BEST BOOK OF THE YEAR “Patricia Evangelista’s searing account is not only the definitive chronicle of a reign of terror in the Philippines, but a warning to the rest of the world about the true dangers of despotism—its nightmarish consequences and its terrible human cost.”—Patrick Radden Keefe, New York Times bestselling author of Empire of Pain “Tragic, elegant, vital . . . Evangelista risked her life to tell this story.”—Tara Westover, #1 New York Times bestselling author of Educated “A journalistic masterpiece”—David Remnick, The New Yorker For six years, journalist Patricia Evangelista documented killings carried out by police and vigilantes in the name of then president Rodrigo Duterte’s war on drugs—a crusade that led to the slaughter of thousands—immersing herself in the world of killers and survivors and capturing the atmosphere of terror created when an elected president decides that some lives are worth less than others. The book takes its title from the words of a vigilante, which demonstrated the psychological accommodation many across the country had made: “I’m really not a bad guy,” he said. “I’m not all bad. Some people need killing.”
